title: El Niño, the Pacific warming that shifts world weather, breaks its daily heat record
summary: The monthly record still stands, but all 674 forecasts point to a winter peak beyond any since 1877 — at a size no seasonal system has been tested against and after summer runs came in 0.3C too warm.

claims.text: Daily Niño 3.4 sea-surface temperature anomaly reached 3.11C as of 21 September 2026, surpassing the previous daily record of 3.08C set on 18 November 2015, calculated using the ONI convention (centered 30-year climatology, NOAA OISSTv2.1).

sources.title: Analysis: ‘Super El Niño’ breaks ‘remarkable’ all-time record

claims.text: August 2026 monthly Niño 3.4 anomaly was around 2.45C, higher than the peak of every prior El Niño on record except 2015-16 (2.75C) and 1877-78 (~2.7C from sparse ship-data reconstruction).

sources.title: Analysis: ‘Super El Niño’ breaks ‘remarkable’ all-time record

claims.text: The 2026 El Niño began in June 2026, reached the strong threshold (>1.5C) by June at 1.6C, exceeded 2C in early July, and has developed faster than any previous event on record.

claims.text: NOAA's Oceanic Niño Index (ONI) uses a rolling centered 30-year average to remove long-term warming; the Relative ONI (RONI), adopted by NOAA CPC in February 2026, subtracts the tropical-mean (20N-20S) anomaly to better isolate ENSO variability.

claims.text: On RONI, daily values stood around 2.5C in mid-September 2026, about 0.7C below the all-time daily RONI record set in late December 1982-83, but were record-setting for that time of year.

claims.text: A 14-model ensemble (674 individual runs) projects a median peak monthly ONI anomaly around 4.1C later in 2026, with 80% of runs between 3.4C and 4.6C, every run above the 2015-16 record, and a margin over that record of ~1.3C larger than the gap between the strongest and fifth-strongest El Niños in 150 years.

sources.title: Analysis: ‘Super El Niño’ breaks ‘remarkable’ all-time record

claims.text: An earlier 667-run analysis projected a median peak of 3.59C (ONI) and 3.1C (RONI) for July-December 2026, with 91% of runs (ONI) and 77% (RONI) exceeding the strongest event in the modern record (2.75C ONI in 2015-16, 2.69C RONI in 1982-83).

claims.text: WMO reported Niño 3.4 averaged +1.5C in May-July 2026 and +2.0C in July, with weekly values +2.2C to +2.6C in late July to mid-August, and subsurface temperatures more than 8C above average in July-early August.

claims.text: NOAA CPC's 10 September 2026 diagnostic reported August Niño 3.4 anomaly +1.8C, Niño 3 +2.5C, Niño 1+2 +3.4C, and subsurface anomalies exceeding +10C at depth.

claims.text: El Niño typically occurs every 2-7 years, lasts 9-12 months, begins developing March-June and peaks November-February, with its largest influence on global temperatures felt in the year after development.

claims.text: The 2023-24 El Niño peaked around 2.0-2.1C on ONI (fifth-highest since 1950) but only ~1.5C on RONI (borderline strong), and the winters of 2024-25 and 2025-26 classified as ENSO-neutral on ONI would be classified as definitive La Niñas on RONI.
